# Cluster {#cluster .unnumbered}

`pyANI-plus` can take advantage of scheduling on High Performance Computing (HPC) clusters, enabling analysis of large datasets. `snakemake` is used to handle and distributed worker jobs providing a uniform framework for running jobs locally (e.g. on your desktop -- the default), or using one of the [Snakemake executor plugins](https://snakemake.github.io/snakemake-plugin-catalog/).

To facilitate this, all ANI compute commands have the `--executor` option (default us `local`)

::: { .callout-note }
Database analysis and plotting commands are only ever run locally.
:::

## SLURM

Slurm is the recommended parallel/HPC executor for `pyANI-plus`. `pyANI-plus` was developed and tested on two SLURM clusters ([ARCHIE-WeSt](https://www.archie-west.ac.uk/) and the [UK Crop Diversity Bioinformatics HPC Resource](https://cropdiversity.ac.uk/)).

To use the `slurm` executor option, a Snakemake configuration file is required. Create a directory containing this `config.yaml` file, and set the `SNAKEMAKE_PROFILE` environment variable to point at that directory. Then, when running `pyANI-plus`, add the `--executor slurm` option, as below.

```bash
mkdir snakemake-profile-name/
emacs snakemake-profile-name/config.yaml  # see examples below
export SNAKEMAKE_PROFILE=$PWD/snakemake-profile-name
pyani-plus ... --executor slurm ...
```

::: { .callout-tip }
If you are using version control for your analysis scripts and/or reproducibility, you should also check-in the `config.yaml` file.
:::

::: { .callout-important }
Some of the underlying ANI tools can be run with multiple cores, but it is best practice to ask the cluster for single-core jobs (each of which has modest memory (RAM) needs). 

The exceptions to this would be `LZ-ANI` and `sourmash`, which are memory demanding but very fast. We run these locally on a single machine (even a desktop) with the default local executor.
:::

### ARCHIE-WeSt

The example below is a configuration used on [ARCHIE-WeSt](https://www.archie-west.ac.uk/) in 2025 while developing the tool.

On this cluster we were limited to at most 400 CPUs. The configuration asks Snakemake to use up to 400 single-core jobs.

The `precommand` is used to make sure the `pyani-plus` command is available and on the `$PATH`. This cluster uses the `module` system for dependencies and to ensure a consistent environment on each node. We used this to make a conda-based package manager available and, within this, we activated a conda environment called `pyani-plus_py312`, which had Python 3.12, `pyani-plus`, and dependencies installed.

```yaml
executor: slurm
jobs: 400
cores: 1
precommand: "module purge && module load miniconda && conda activate pyani-plus_py312"

default-resources:
    slurm_partition: dev
    slurm_account: <ACCOUNTNAME>
```

This cluster has a billing system and required explicitly declaration of the partition (queue) and account (here masked as `ACCOUNTNAME`. The RAM limit is implicit (set by the cluster administrators as a multiple of the cores for billing purposes, on this system).

### Crop Diversity

This configuration was used on the [Crop Diversity Cluster](https://cropdiversity.ac.uk) in 2025 and 2026 for large sets of bacterial genomes. It targeted the `hicpu` queue for low-memory CPU limited jobs, which at the time was setup with older compute nodes with 6 hour runtime and 2GB RAM upper limits. On this HPC we were permitted to run 1000 jobs simultaneously. 

```yaml
executor: slurm
jobs: 1000
cores: 1

default-resources:
    slurm_partition: hicpu
    slurm_account: <ACCOUNTNAME>
    runtime: 100
```

Snakemake would give distracting warnings if the account or runtime was omitted, even though this cluster had default values setup in SLURM.

By default the cluster applied a 1GB memory limit, which was ample for bacteria. Adding `memory: 2G` or `mem_mb: 2048` under the `default-resources` section would have used the full 2G RAM limit on this queue to handle _slightly_ larger genomes.

The following configuration was used in 2026 for a set of 100 fungal genomes of around 40Mbp (the total run taking less than a day). Here individual comparisons naturally take longer than with bacteria, so a queue with a longer run-time limit had to be used (24 hour, or 1440 mins).

While most of the comparisons worked with 4GB of RAM, a few needed more, so about 5GB was requested:

```yaml
executor: slurm
jobs: 1000
cores: 1

default-resources:
    slurm_partition: medium
    slurm_account: <ACCOUNTNAME>
    runtime: 1440
    mem_mb: 5000
    threads: 1
```

## Cluster Troubleshooting Tips

- Start with a small example first, like the walkthough, to make sure the cluster intergration is working.
- Check the stdout/stderr logs if possible. 
- Use the logging and debug options within the tool (to keep the intermediate files and logs).

- If you suspect specfic genomes or genome pairs to be a problem, try reducing the number of genomes to work out which.

- If you are getting out of memory (OOM) failures, this could be due to larger or more complex genomes - in which case try increasing the RAM limit. 
- Pathological data, such as genomes that have not been quality controlled, can cause problems in some methods (eg excessive runs of N). 
- On SLURM the `sacct` command or similar will show when a job failed with `OUT_OF_MEMORY`. In these cases, adjust your Snakemake `config.yaml` and retry (see example above).
